name: Ishoyahb III
otherNames: Ishoyahb of Adiabene; Isho'-yahbh of Adiabene, in E. A. Wallis Budge's English of Thomas of Marga
Iso'yahb, in Rubens Duval's Latin edition of his letters
Jesujabus Adiabenus, in J. S. Assemani's Latin; Yesu'yahb Adiabenus, in the Latin of Elias of Nisibis
Jesujabus hazzensis, "of Hazza", the region Amr ibn Matta says is now called Arbela, in the Latin of Amr and of Mari ibn Sulayman
Isô'yahb d'Adiabène, in Addai Scher's French of the Chronicle of Seert
knownFor: Ishoyahb III of Adiabene was catholicos, or head, of the Church of the East in the first years of Arab rule. His surviving letters fight the teaching of his friend Sahdona and the bishops of Fars and Qatar who broke from him.
dates: Elected catholicos between 647 and 650 and died between 657 and 660, by the witnesses' differing counts. No source gives his birth or his age
place: Kuphlana in Adiabene, his home village, by Thomas of Marga; the school of Nisibis; Nineveh, or Mosul, as bishop; Arbela and Mosul as metropolitan; al-Mada'in, where he was made catholicos; Beth Abe near Mosul, his monastery, where Mari ibn Sulayman places his burial
tradition: The Church of the East on the Silk Road
role: Catholicos of the Church of the East; before that bishop of Nineveh and metropolitan, the senior bishop, of Arbela and Mosul

keyWorks.title: Letters
keyWorks.about: 106 letters (the scan reads "evi") in three parts, written as bishop, as metropolitan and as catholicos, Rubens Duval says. They survive in one Vatican manuscript, which Assemani dated to the 900s and Duval thinks may be from the late 700s. Held in Duval's Latin (1905), with two passages in Alphonse Mingana's English (1926)

keyWorks.title: Order of the church's daily services
keyWorks.about: Amr ibn Matta says he set the order of the office for the year's round, as it still stood in Amr's day. Thomas of Marga says that before him the services were done in a confused way everywhere, and that the monk 'Anan-isho' arranged the canons of the Hudhra, the book of the year's services, at his bidding

keyWorks.title: Rites
keyWorks.about: orders of baptism, of the consecration of an altar and of the absolution of apostates and heretics, among others, which Duval lists from manuscripts. Duval adds that a baptism liturgy Assemani gave to Ishoyahb I may perhaps be his. No held text of these rites carries his name

traces: The school he built at Kuphlana, his home village, after the monks of Beth Abe left rather than live beside it, by Thomas of Marga.
A golden Book of the Gospels that he left to Beth Abe, Thomas says.
His deathbed words, in Thomas of Marga and Amr ibn Matta. He said George should follow him without saying which of his two disciples named George he meant, and the two quarreled.
His letter on India. Later writers on Christianity in India, among them Henry Yule, Thomas Whitehouse, G. T. Mackenzie and Mingana, cite it as early evidence for bishops in India.
remembered: Thomas of Marga calls him "the blessed in everything".
Mari ibn Sulayman, writing in the 1100s, says that in his time many teachers flourished and church annals began to be written.
Amr ibn Matta, in the 1300s, calls him learned and upright, strong in faith and zeal, but of a crooked temper.
Duval calls the letters an outstanding example of Syriac letter-writing, from the age when Syriac was still pure.

uncertain: Much of his story comes from late or partisan witnesses. Thomas of Marga wrote the history of Beth Abe, his own monastery, in 840, about two centuries after him, and parts of it rest on legend and house tradition. Amr ibn Matta and Mari ibn Sulayman wrote their lives of the patriarchs in the 1300s and 1100s. Bar Hebraeus, in the 1200s, wrote for the rival Syriac Orthodox church.

The eagle vision and the stolen casket. Thomas of Marga sets the vision on the night the monks left. He says Ishoyahb stole a marble casket of apostles' bones at Antioch, resting it on tradition handed down in his monastery.

The peace mission to Heraclius. Thomas of Marga says Ishoyahb, then bishop of Nineveh, went with the catholicos Ishoyahb II of Gedhala and with Sahdona, and Duval puts the journey in 630. The Khuzistan chronicle, written about 660, names Cyriacus of Nisibis, Gabriel of Karkha and Marutha of Gustra as the catholicos's companions and does not name him. The Chronicle of Seert names no companions.

Who sent the mission. Thomas of Marga says King Sheroe. The Khuzistan chronicle and the Chronicle of Seert say Queen Boran. Budge, who translated Thomas in 1893, and Addai Scher, who translated Seert in 1919, both side with Boran.

Sahdona. Thomas of Marga says Sahdona's faith was turned at Apamea on the mission, and that Ishoyahb, as catholicos, later expelled him. The Chronicle of Seert says Ishoyahb, then metropolitan, rebuked his friend, and that the catholicos Maremmeh condemned Sahdona at a synod at Karkha. Scher places the turn in Persia, not at Apamea. Duval says Ishoyahb's letters were the real cause of Sahdona's removal.

His election. Amr ibn Matta says the bishops, fearing he would seize the throne, left the choice to him, and he named himself. Mari ibn Sulayman says only that the electors chose him. In his own letter to Isaac of Nisibis on his election, Ishoyahb calls himself a frail man (Duval's Latin).

The year of his election. Amr ibn Matta gives the fifth year of the caliph Uthman and the Greek year 962. Elias of Nisibis gives Uthman's fourth year. Assemani reckons Uthman's fifth year as 650. T. J. Lamy, editing Bar Hebraeus in 1877, gives 647 or 648, against Assemani. Budge gives 647, and Eduard Sachau's 1915 note gives his years as 647 to 658. Mingana, Mackenzie, Yule and Martin Jugie give 650. Duval's year for Maremmeh's death cannot be read in the scan.
His years in office. Elias of Nisibis gives nine years and three months. Amr ibn Matta's scan seems to read seven years and three months, and in another line forty-five years of service.

The year of his death. Duval gives 658, and Budge 657 or 658. Amr ibn Matta gives the Greek year 971, and Elias of Nisibis the third year of the caliph Ali. Assemani gives 660, followed by Mingana, Yule, Whitehouse, Mackenzie and Jugie. Lamy says he died before 660, while Denha was maphrian, the Syriac Orthodox church's head in the East. Bar Hebraeus gives no year.
His burial. Mari ibn Sulayman places it at Beth Abe in the district of Mosul. Amr ibn Matta's line is garbled in the scan, naming both al-Mada'in and Mar Jacob, the founder of Beth Abe.

Bar Hebraeus says he spent much money on gifts to judges to stop the Syriac Orthodox building a church at Mosul. This is a rival church's charge. Lamy notes that Ishoyahb tells the affair himself in a letter to Gabriel, and Duval says he fought the Jacobites, as the Syriac Orthodox were called, a great deal as metropolitan.

The break with Simeon of Rev-Ardashir. His letters show the quarrel still open, and he sent bishops to Fars and Qatar to win the rebel bishops back or declare them cut off. Mari ibn Sulayman says Ishoyahb went himself and brought Simeon to obedience. Budge says the reasons for the dispute are little known.

The place at the far end of India in the letter. Duval reads Qalah and Mingana Kalah, which Mingana links with Ceylon. Assemani reads Colon, which Yule, Whitehouse and Mackenzie take as Quilon. Henri Cordier, Mingana reports, put it near Malacca.

The people who left the faith. Duval reads Mazunaye, and Mingana places them in Mazon, in Oman. Assemani reads Maruanitae and takes them as people of Merv. Ishoyahb writes that the Arabs did not force them to leave their faith, only to give up half their goods.
No early source ties him to the mission that reached China in 635. Assemani puts that mission under Ishoyahb II of Gedhala. The Chronicle of Seert's chapter on Ishoyahb III is lost.
